<div class="intro-box">
<strong>How to use this guide:</strong> Each project below has a <strong>between-subjects</strong> and <strong>within-subjects</strong> variant. All use a two-condition design testable with an independent or paired t-test. All are designed to be completable in one lab session (~20 participants, ~5–10 min per participant) with minimal/free materials.<br><br>
<strong>These study plans show the shape and size of a good group project!</strong> You do not need to get any more complex than this, and marks are <strong>NOT</strong> related to complexity — usually, the other way around!

📚 **Suggested readings for all projects** are available in the <a href="https://learn.gold.ac.uk/mod/folder/view.php?id=1795121" target="_blank"><strong>Project Articles folder on Learn.gold</strong></a>.
</div>

# Projects

<details class="project-card" open>
<summary>
<span class="project-letter">A</span>
<div class="project-info">
<div class="project-title">The Effect of Smiling on Perceived Approachability</div>
<div class="project-meta"><span class="tag tag-social">Social</span> <span class="tag tag-effect-lg">Effect: Medium–Large</span></div>
</div>
<span class="chevron">&#9654;</span>
</summary>
<div class="project-body">

**Background:** Facial expressions are powerful social signals. Research consistently shows that smiling faces are rated as more approachable, trustworthy, and warm than neutral faces (Hess et al., 2000). This is a robust social perception effect with clear theoretical grounding in evolutionary psychology and social cognition.

<div class="iv-dv">
<strong>IV:</strong> Facial expression (neutral vs smiling)<br>
<strong>DV:</strong> Approachability rating (1–7 Likert scale, averaged across faces)
</div>

### Between-subjects variant

- Group 1 rates **8 photos of people with neutral expressions** on approachability (1 = not at all, 7 = very approachable)
- Group 2 rates the **same 8 people with smiling expressions** on approachability
- Photos matched for age, gender balance (4 male, 4 female), and attractiveness
- Different participants in each condition

### Within-subjects variant

- All participants rate **16 photos**: 8 with neutral expressions and 8 with smiling expressions (different people in each set, matched for age/gender)
- Photos presented in randomised order
- DV is mean approachability rating for neutral vs smiling faces (within-participant comparison)

**Materials:** 16 printed photos (or PowerPoint slides), rating sheets, pens. Photos sourced from open-access face databases (e.g., Chicago Face Database, Radboud Faces Database).

**Expected effect:** Medium-to-large (*d* ≈ 0.6–1.0). Smiling-approachability effect is very robust across cultures.

<div class="readings">

**Indicative readings:**

Hess, U., Adams, R. B., & Kleck, R. E. (2000). Facial appearance, gender, and emotion expression. *Emotion*, 5(1), 119–124.

Willis, J., & Todorov, A. (2006). First impressions: Making up your mind after a 100-ms exposure to a face. *Psychological Science*, 17(7), 592–598.

</div>
</div>
</details>

<details class="project-card">
<summary>
<span class="project-letter">B</span>
<div class="project-info">
<div class="project-title">The Effect of Background Music on Concentration</div>
<div class="project-meta"><span class="tag tag-cognitive">Cognitive</span> <span class="tag tag-effect-md">Effect: Medium</span></div>
</div>
<span class="chevron">&#9654;</span>
</summary>
<div class="project-body">

**Background:** The irrelevant sound effect (Salamé & Baddeley, 1989) demonstrates that background sound impairs serial recall. Music with lyrics is particularly disruptive due to phonological interference. Well-established effect with reasonable effect sizes.

<div class="iv-dv">
<strong>IV:</strong> Sound condition (silence vs music with lyrics)<br>
<strong>DV:</strong> Number of items correctly recalled in serial order (out of 10–15)
</div>

### Between-subjects variant

- Group 1 studies a list of 15 words in **silence**
- Group 2 studies the same list while **pop music with lyrics** plays from a speaker
- 2-minute study period → 1-minute distractor → 2-minute written recall
- Different participants in each condition

### Within-subjects variant

- All participants study **two different word lists** (counterbalanced order), one in silence, one with music
- Lists matched for word frequency and concreteness
- Same timing structure
- Each participant provides two recall scores

**Materials:** 2 word lists (printed), portable speaker, music track (pre-selected), recall sheets, pens

**Expected effect:** Medium (*d* ≈ 0.5–0.7). Irrelevant sound effect is well-replicated.

<div class="readings">

**Indicative readings:**

Salamé, P., & Baddeley, A. (1989). Effects of background music on phonological short-term memory. *Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology*, 41A, 107–122.

Perham, N., & Vizard, J. (2011). Can preference for background music mediate the irrelevant sound effect? *Applied Cognitive Psychology*, 25(4), 625–631.

</div>
</div>
</details>

<details class="project-card">
<summary>
<span class="project-letter">C</span>
<div class="project-info">
<div class="project-title">The Effect of Colour on Memory for Words</div>
<div class="project-meta"><span class="tag tag-cognitive">Cognitive</span> <span class="tag tag-effect-sm">Effect: Small–Medium</span></div>
</div>
<span class="chevron">&#9654;</span>
</summary>
<div class="project-body">

**Background:** The Von Restorff isolation effect and colour-attention research suggest that words presented in colour (especially red) are better remembered than words in black. Practical, visual manipulation that's easy to set up.

<div class="iv-dv">
<strong>IV:</strong> Word colour (black text vs red text)<br>
<strong>DV:</strong> Number of words correctly recalled (out of 15–20)
</div>

### Between-subjects variant

- Group 1 studies a list of 20 words printed in **black ink**
- Group 2 studies the same list printed in **red ink**
- 2-minute study → 1-minute distractor → 2-minute free recall
- Different participants in each condition

### Within-subjects variant

- All participants study **one list of 20 words**: 10 in black, 10 in red (randomly intermixed)
- DV is number of red words recalled vs number of black words recalled (within-participant comparison)
- Same timing structure

**Materials:** Printed word lists (colour printer needed for red version), recall sheets, pens

**Expected effect:** Small-to-medium (*d* ≈ 0.3–0.5). Colour effects are often found but magnitude varies.

<div class="readings">

**Indicative readings:**

Dzulkifli, M. A., & Mustafar, M. F. (2013). The influence of colour on memory performance: A review. *Malaysian Journal of Medical Sciences*, 20(2), 3–9.

Kuhbandner, C., & Pekrun, R. (2013). Joint effects of emotion and color on memory. *Emotion*, 13(3), 375–379.

</div>
</div>
</details>

<details class="project-card">
<summary>
<span class="project-letter">D</span>
<div class="project-info">
<div class="project-title">The Effect of Imagery on Word Recall</div>
<div class="project-meta"><span class="tag tag-cognitive">Cognitive</span> <span class="tag tag-effect-lg">Effect: Medium–Large</span></div>
</div>
<span class="chevron">&#9654;</span>
</summary>
<div class="project-body">

**Background:** Paivio's dual coding theory (1971) predicts that forming mental images of words leads to better recall than rote repetition, because information is encoded in both verbal and visual systems. One of the most robust effects in memory research.

<div class="iv-dv">
<strong>IV:</strong> Learning instruction (rote repetition vs mental imagery)<br>
<strong>DV:</strong> Number of words correctly recalled (out of 15–20)
</div>

### Between-subjects variant

- Group 1 told to **repeat each word silently** as they study the list
- Group 2 told to **form a vivid mental image** of each word as they study
- Same word list (concrete nouns), 2-minute study → 1-minute distractor → 2-minute recall
- Different participants in each condition

### Within-subjects variant

- All participants study **two different word lists** (counterbalanced)
- List A: instructed to use rote repetition
- List B: instructed to use mental imagery
- Same timing structure
- Each participant provides two recall scores

**Materials:** 2 word lists of concrete nouns (printed), instruction sheets, recall sheets, pens

**Expected effect:** Medium-to-large (*d* ≈ 0.6–1.0). Dual coding is one of the most reliable effects in cognitive psychology.

<div class="readings">

**Indicative readings:**

Paivio, A. (1971). *Imagery and verbal processes*. Holt, Rinehart & Winston.

Bower, G. H. (1970). Imagery as a relational organizer in associative learning. *Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior*, 9(5), 529–533.

</div>
</div>
</details>

<details class="project-card">
<summary>
<span class="project-letter">E</span>
<div class="project-info">
<div class="project-title">The Effect of Phone Presence on Attention</div>
<div class="project-meta"><span class="tag tag-social">Social</span> <span class="tag tag-cognitive">Cognitive</span> <span class="tag tag-effect-sm">Effect: Small–Medium</span></div>
</div>
<span class="chevron">&#9654;</span>
</summary>
<div class="project-body">

**Background:** The "brain drain" hypothesis (Ward et al., 2017) suggests that the mere visible presence of a smartphone — even switched off — reduces available cognitive capacity because people must actively resist attending to it. A highly contemporary topic with strong student engagement.

<div class="iv-dv">
<strong>IV:</strong> Phone presence (phone visible on desk vs phone out of sight)<br>
<strong>DV:</strong> Score on a short attention/concentration task (e.g., digit span or proofreading accuracy)
</div>

### Between-subjects variant

- Group 1 completes a concentration task with their **phone placed face-down on the desk** in front of them
- Group 2 completes the same task with their **phone in their bag/pocket** (out of sight)
- Task: proofread a short passage and circle errors (10 deliberate errors), or complete a digit span task
- Different participants in each condition

### Within-subjects variant

- All participants complete **two equivalent tasks** (counterbalanced): one with phone on desk, one with phone in bag
- Tasks matched for difficulty (e.g., two different passages with same number of errors)
- Each participant provides two accuracy scores

**Materials:** Printed proofreading passages (or digit span sheets), answer sheets, pens. Participants use their own phones.

**Expected effect:** Small-to-medium (*d* ≈ 0.3–0.5). Effect is debated but consistently found in some paradigms — good for discussion either way.

<div class="readings">

**Indicative readings:**

Ward, A. F., Duke, K., Gneezy, A., & Bos, M. W. (2017). Brain drain: The mere presence of one's own smartphone reduces available cognitive capacity. *Journal of the Association for Consumer Research*, 2(2), 140–154.

Thornton, B., Faires, A., Robbins, M., & Rollins, E. (2014). The mere presence of a cell phone may be distracting. *Social Psychology*, 45(6), 479–488.

</div>
</div>
</details>

<details class="project-card">
<summary>
<span class="project-letter">F</span>
<div class="project-info">
<div class="project-title">The Effect of Testing on Learning (Retrieval Practice)</div>
<div class="project-meta"><span class="tag tag-cognitive">Cognitive</span> <span class="tag tag-effect-lg">Effect: Medium–Large</span></div>
</div>
<span class="chevron">&#9654;</span>
</summary>
<div class="project-body">

**Background:** The testing effect (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006) shows that actively retrieving information from memory improves long-term retention more than re-studying. Extremely robust finding with practical implications for student learning.

<div class="iv-dv">
<strong>IV:</strong> Study method (re-study vs retrieval practice)<br>
<strong>DV:</strong> Number of facts correctly recalled on final test (out of 10–15)
</div>

### Between-subjects variant

- Both groups read a short factual passage (2 minutes)
- Group 1: **re-reads** the passage for another 2 minutes
- Group 2: spends 2 minutes **answering recall questions** about the passage (no feedback)
- 2-minute delay → final recall test (same questions for both groups)

### Within-subjects variant

- All participants read **two short passages** (counterbalanced)
- Passage A: followed by re-study
- Passage B: followed by retrieval practice (recall questions)
- Final test on both passages after delay
- Each participant provides two recall scores

**Materials:** 2 factual passages, practice recall questions, final test sheets, pens

**Expected effect:** Medium-to-large (*d* ≈ 0.5–0.8). Testing effect is very robust even at short delays.

<div class="readings">

**Indicative readings:**

Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. *Psychological Science*, 17(3), 249–255.

Rowland, C. A. (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review. *Psychological Bulletin*, 140(6), 1432–1463.

</div>
</div>
</details>

<details class="project-card">
<summary>
<span class="project-letter">G</span>
<div class="project-info">
<div class="project-title">The Effect of Social Presence on Task Performance</div>
<div class="project-meta"><span class="tag tag-social">Social</span> <span class="tag tag-effect-md">Effect: Small–Medium</span></div>
</div>
<span class="chevron">&#9654;</span>
</summary>
<div class="project-body">

**Background:** Zajonc's (1965) drive theory of social facilitation predicts that the presence of others enhances performance on simple/well-learned tasks but impairs performance on complex/novel tasks. One of the oldest findings in social psychology, with a clear theoretical framework and straightforward manipulation.

<div class="iv-dv">
<strong>IV:</strong> Social condition (alone vs observed)<br>
<strong>DV:</strong> Number of items completed correctly on a simple task (e.g., easy anagrams or basic arithmetic)
</div>

### Between-subjects variant

- Group 1 completes 20 easy anagrams (5-letter words) **alone in a room**
- Group 2 completes the same anagrams while being **watched by two confederates** (seated nearby, observing silently)
- 3-minute time limit
- Different participants in each condition

### Within-subjects variant

- All participants complete **two sets of 20 anagrams** (counterbalanced): one alone, one while observed
- Sets matched for difficulty
- Each participant provides two accuracy/speed scores

**Materials:** Printed anagram sheets, answer sheets, pens, timer. 2 confederates needed for "observed" condition.

**Expected effect:** Small-to-medium (*d* ≈ 0.3–0.6). Effect is reliable for simple tasks; may reverse for complex tasks — excellent for discussion.

<div class="readings">

**Indicative readings:**

Zajonc, R. B. (1965). Social facilitation. *Science*, 149(3681), 269–274.

Bond, C. F., & Titus, L. J. (1983). Social facilitation: A meta-analysis of 241 studies. *Psychological Bulletin*, 94(2), 265–292.

</div>
</div>
</details>

<details class="project-card">
<summary>
<span class="project-letter">H</span>
<div class="project-info">
<div class="project-title">The Effect of Anchoring on Numerical Estimates</div>
<div class="project-meta"><span class="tag tag-social">Social</span> <span class="tag tag-cognitive">Cognitive</span> <span class="tag tag-effect-lg">Effect: Large</span></div>
</div>
<span class="chevron">&#9654;</span>
</summary>
<div class="project-body">

**Background:** Tversky and Kahneman's (1974) anchoring and adjustment heuristic shows that exposure to an arbitrary number biases subsequent numerical estimates, even when the anchor is clearly irrelevant. One of the most robust findings in judgment and decision-making, with strong real-world implications (pricing, negotiations, sentencing).

<div class="iv-dv">
<strong>IV:</strong> Anchor value (high vs low)<br>
<strong>DV:</strong> Mean numerical estimate across a set of questions
</div>

### Between-subjects variant

- Both groups answer 8 general knowledge estimation questions (e.g., "How many countries are in Africa?")
- Group 1 first sees a **high anchor** for each question (e.g., "More or fewer than 120?")
- Group 2 first sees a **low anchor** for each question (e.g., "More or fewer than 15?")
- Participants decide more/fewer, then give their own estimate
- Different participants in each condition

### Within-subjects variant

- All participants answer **16 questions**: 8 with high anchors, 8 with low anchors (randomised order)
- Questions matched for difficulty across the two sets
- DV is mean estimate for high-anchor questions vs mean estimate for low-anchor questions

**Materials:** Printed questionnaire sheets, pens. No technology required.

**Expected effect:** Large (*d* ≈ 0.8–1.2). Anchoring is one of the most robust effects in cognitive psychology — almost always significant.

<div class="readings">

**Indicative readings:**

Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. *Science*, 185(4157), 1124–1131.

Furnham, A., & Boo, H. C. (2011). A literature review of the anchoring effect. *Journal of Socio-Economics*, 40(1), 35–42.

</div>
</div>
</details>

<details class="project-card">
<summary>
<span class="project-letter">I</span>
<div class="project-info">
<div class="project-title">The Effect of Name Type on Competence Ratings</div>
<div class="project-meta"><span class="tag tag-social">Social</span> <span class="tag tag-effect-md">Effect: Small–Medium</span></div>
</div>
<span class="chevron">&#9654;</span>
</summary>
<div class="project-body">

**Background:** Research on name-based stereotyping shows that identical CVs or descriptions receive different evaluations depending on the name attached. This taps into implicit social cognition and stereotyping — a topic students find compelling and which generates strong discussions about bias, fairness, and ecological validity.

<div class="iv-dv">
<strong>IV:</strong> Name type (stereotypically "traditional/formal" vs "modern/informal" first names)<br>
<strong>DV:</strong> Mean competence rating (1–7 Likert scale, averaged across rated dimensions)
</div>

### Between-subjects variant

- Both groups read **4 identical short professional profiles** (e.g., job applicant descriptions)
- Group 1 profiles have **traditional names** (e.g., Elizabeth, James, Margaret, William)
- Group 2 profiles have **modern/informal names** (e.g., Jayden, Destiny, Kai, Skye)
- Participants rate each profile on competence, professionalism, and likely success (1–7)
- Different participants in each condition

### Within-subjects variant

- All participants rate **8 profiles**: 4 with traditional names, 4 with modern names (randomised order)
- Profiles are different people but matched for qualifications and experience
- DV is mean competence rating for traditional vs modern names (within-participant comparison)

**Materials:** Printed profiles and rating sheets, pens. Profiles need careful construction to be realistic and matched.

**Expected effect:** Small-to-medium (*d* ≈ 0.3–0.6). Effects are typically found but can be moderated by participant demographics — good for discussion.

<div class="readings">

**Indicative readings:**

Bertrand, M., & Mullainathan, S. (2004). Are Emily and Greg more employable than Lakisha and Jamal? A field experiment on labor market discrimination. *American Economic Review*, 94(4), 991–1013.

Erwin, P. G. (2006). Children's evaluative stereotypes of masculine, feminine, and androgynous first names. *The Psychological Record*, 56(4), 513–519.

</div>
</div>
